CISA KEV: CVE-2008-4128 — Cisco IOS Cross-Site Request Forgery Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-07-13 1 use case 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

Cisco IOS 12.4 contains multiple cross-site forgery vulnerabilities that allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via (1) a certain "show privilege" command to the /level/15/exec/- URI, and (2) a certain "alias exec" command to the /level/15/exec/-/configure/http URI. Vendor: Cisco, Product: IOS. Federal patch due: 2026-07-16.

jscrambler npm package publishes malicious preinstall binary

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 15 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 11, 2026, version 8.14.0 of jscrambler was published to npm carrying a malicious preinstall hook that drops and executes a platform-specific native binary on Linux, Windows, and macOS. jscrambler is the official CLI client for the Jscrambler Code Integrity API, a commercial JavaScript obfuscation and web-app protection service, with a clean version history dating back to 0.1.0. The compromised release was flagged by StepSecurity's AI Release Analyzer with a suspicion score of 0 (the maximum suspicion rating) on publish.

Compromised jscrambler npm package (8.14.0+) artifacts written to node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for on-disk artifacts of the trojanized jscrambler npm release: the 7.8 MB dist/intro.js binary container written under node_modules/jscrambler and the extracted per-platform stealer payload hashes. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact package path, the disguised container file, and the three published payload SHA256s. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact IOC matrix: node_modules/jscrambler/dist/intro.js and the three extracted payload SHA256s. Corroborated by Socket.dev and The Hacker News, which confirmed the same package/path and Rust-compiled cross-platform stealer. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019f5225-a834-719b-9b66-c82edd147d7c

npm/node preinstall drops and executes hidden native binary from OS temp dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the core execution step: the jscrambler preinstall loader (dist/setup.js) decompresses a platform binary to a randomly named dotfile in the OS temp directory and launches it detached from the npm install tree. Detects node/npm spawning an executable whose path is a hidden dotfile under Temp or /tmp. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's loader behaviour: preinstall reads dist/intro.js and spawns a randomly named dotfile in the OS temp dir (.[a-z0-9]{6,} with .exe on Windows) detached from npm. Parent=node/npm + hidden temp binary is extremely rare in benign builds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.003 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit native postinstall tools (esbuild, node-sass, sharp) extracting prebuilt binaries to temp — but those are not hidden dotfiles
  • node-based test harnesses that shell out to a scratch temp binary
  • Electron/pkg self-extracting apps unpacking to temp on first run
  • Yarn/pnpm build steps writing temp helper executables (rarely dotfiles)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("esbuild","node-sass","node-gyp","sharp","electron-builder"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the temp file path and SHA256, confirm parent is node/npm during an install window, and check if jscrambler 8.14.0+ is present. 2) Contain: kill the detached temp process, quarantine the temp binary, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pull the process's outbound connections (Tor/C2 IPs), look for browser credential-store and .npmrc file access, and enumerate other hosts that installed the same package version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node")
| where FolderPath has_any ("Temp","/tmp/")
| where FileName startswith "."
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FolderPath has "/tmp/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where NewProcessName has "Temp"
| extend LeafName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where LeafName startswith "." and LeafName endswith ".exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Execution of extracted jscrambler stealer payload by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on any process launched from one of the three published, extracted stealer payloads (ELF/PE32+/Mach-O) regardless of file name or drop path, catching the payload even if the loader randomizes its temp filename. Rationale: Uses the three exact payload SHA256s from the IOC table; hash-based execution detection survives the loader's random temp filename and is near-zero FP. Second-sourced as a Rust cross-platform infostealer by The Hacker News/Socket. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html

Stealer C2 egress to Tor Project infrastructure and hardcoded IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections from a developer/CI host to the two hardcoded stealer C2 IPs and the check/archive.torproject.org endpoints the dropped binary contacts. High-fidelity because these are specific attacker-tied indicators, not generic Tor usage. Rationale: Uses the exact C2 IPs (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) and torproject.org endpoints named in the Harden-Runner analysis and independently confirmed by second sources. Any dev host reaching these is high-signal for the stealer's C2. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html

  • Security research replaying the C2 IPs in a lab
  • Threat-intel enrichment jobs actively probing the IOC IPs

npm/node install spawns reconnaissance or shell utilities AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the preinstall execution phase where the compromised package's install context spawns local shells or host-recon tools — deviation from normal build behaviour. Reviewer-requested; grounded in the article's automatic preinstall-hook execution during npm install. Rationale: The article confirms the malicious code runs automatically via the npm preinstall hook; recon/download tools spawned by node/npm during install are anomalous for a JS-obfuscation CLI build and map to the stealer's discovery/staging behaviour reported by second sources (env/.npmrc/cloud-cred collection). Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1087 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD build scripts that legitimately call curl/wget to fetch assets during install
  • node-based tooling invoking net.exe/reg.exe for environment setup
  • postinstall scripts running hostname/ipconfig for telemetry
  • cross-platform build tools shelling out to sh/uname on Linux runners
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install","electron","cypress","playwright install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent npm/node command line and the package being installed; confirm whether jscrambler 8.14.0+ (or another unexpected package) is in the tree. 2) Contain: if unexpected, isolate the host and halt the CI job. 3) Hunt: pivot to any hidden temp binary spawned by the same node process, C2 egress, and access to .npmrc / browser credential stores.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node","npm")
| where FileName in~ ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","reg.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami","hostname","id","uname","curl","wget")
| summarize ChildCount = dcount(FileName), Children = make_set(FileName), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where ChildCount >= 1
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| extend Child = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where Child in~ ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","reg.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| summarize ChildCount = dcount(Child), Children = make_set(Child) by Computer, SubjectUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where ChildCount >= 1
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm/node install spawns recon or shell utility
id: c1d8e4b2-9a37-4f6c-8b1d-3e7a2c0f9d61
description: Detects node/npm spawning host-reconnaissance or download utilities during package installation, matching malicious preinstall behaviour
references:

detection:

  condition: selection

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.exe) @Image:(*\\whoami.exe OR *\\systeminfo.exe OR *\\net.exe OR *\\net1.exe OR *\\hostname.exe OR *\\ipconfig.exe OR *\\reg.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process_name) as children from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","node","npm") AND Processes.process_name IN ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","reg.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami","hostname","id","uname","curl","wget") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where mvcount(children) >= 1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process_name) as children from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","node","npm") AND Processes.process_name IN ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","reg.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami","hostname","id","uname","curl","wget") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where mvcount(children) >= 1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Persistence created by hidden temp-dir binary (scheduled task / Run key) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the stealer establishing persistence: a hidden binary running from the OS temp directory spawning schtasks.exe or writing a Run-key/registry autostart. Grounded in the article's temp-dotfile drop and corroborated persistence (Windows scheduled task / macOS LaunchAgent) reported by second sources. Rationale: Chains the article's temp-dotfile binary (from the IOC table) to the persistence step confirmed by second sources (Windows scheduled task / macOS LaunchAgent). Parent = hidden temp binary spawning schtasks/reg is a rare, high-fidelity persistence pivot distinct from the drop/exec UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate temp-extracted installer registering a scheduled task on first run
  • Software updaters writing a Run key from a temp staging binary
  • Admin scripting that creates scheduled tasks from a temp-located tool
  • EDR/RMM agents bootstrapping persistence from a temp path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("Packages","WindowsApps","Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the scheduled-task/Run-key target and the parent temp binary hash; confirm parent is a hidden dotfile. 2) Contain: delete the persistence entry, quarantine the temp binary, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check for the payload SHA256, C2 egress to the known IPs/Tor domains, and jscrambler 8.14.0+ across the fleet; on macOS look for a matching LaunchAgent plist.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Temp"
| extend ParentLeaf = tostring(split(InitiatingProcessFolderPath, "\\")[-1])
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "."
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create")
   or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "Run")
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("New-ScheduledTask","CurrentVersion\\Run"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has "Temp"
| extend ParentLeaf = tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where ParentLeaf startswith "."
| extend Child = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where (Child =~ "schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "/create")
   or (Child =~ "reg.exe" and CommandLine has "Run")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hidden temp-dir binary establishes persistence via schtasks or Run key
id: a5f2c8d1-7b40-4e93-9c6a-2d1b8e0f4a72
description: Detects a hidden dotfile binary in the OS temp directory spawning schtasks /create or writing a registry Run key, matching jscrambler stealer persistence
references:

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2

| CommandLine=/(\/create|\\Run)/i

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_path="*\\Temp\\.*" AND Processes.process_name IN ("schtasks.exe","reg.exe","powershell.exe") AND (Processes.process="*create*" OR Processes.process="*\\Run*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_path Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_path="*\\Temp\\.*" AND Processes.process_name IN ("schtasks.exe","reg.exe","powershell.exe") AND (Processes.process="*create*" OR Processes.process="*\\Run*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_path Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injective npm Supply Chain Attack: 18 Packages Backdoored to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 9 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 8, 2026, attackers used access to a trusted developer's account to slip a backdoor into a widely used software development kit for the Injective blockchain. Disguised as harmless analytics, the code quietly captured wallet recovery phrases and private keys and sent them to an attacker-controlled server the moment a wallet was created or loaded. Automatic publishing pushed the tainted code out to 18 related packages within minutes, and it stayed live for less than an hour before being pulled and fixed. If your application installed any of the affected packages during that window, or pic…

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Injective npm Supply Chain Attack: 18 Packages Backdoored to Steal Crypto Wallet
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 payload file dropped on disk · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Injective SDK wallet-key exfil to lookalike domain testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Injective SDK wallet-key exfil to lookalike domain testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound resolution/connection to the attacker-controlled exfil host that the backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 reassembles from an obfuscated char-code array and POSTs stolen seed phrases / private keys to (carried base64 in the X-Request-Id header). The FQDN is a lookalike of legitimate Injective gRPC-Web infra but is not a real Injective endpoint, so exact-host contact is high fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the exact FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network decoded from the char-code array (_e/_d) in key-derivation-telemetry.ts; cross-checked against BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and SlowMist which all cite this host as the POST destination for the base64 secret in the X-Request-Id header. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/injective-labs-github-compromise-pushes.html • https://slowmist.medium.com/threat-intelligence-injective-sdk-compromised-crypto-wallet-private-keys-stolen-0b8f06bf37ad • https://crypto.news/compromised-injective-sdk-sends-wallet-keys-through-fake-telemetry/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1132.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI runner still on the backdoored 1.20.21 build genuinely beaconing (this is a true positive, not an FP)
  • Malware sandbox / detonation VM replaying the sample and resolving the IOC
  • Threat-intel scanner or DNS sinkhole appliance resolving the indicator during enrichment
  • Security researcher manually curling the host to confirm it is live
Suppression filter
// scope to the SDK runtime to drop scanner/appliance noise
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","electron.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the initiating process (expect node.exe/electron.exe or a browser running a wallet/DEX frontend); pull the app's package-lock/node_modules to confirm @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 is present. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and force-rotate every wallet seed phrase and private key that host touched — treat all as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for the malicious file (key-derivation-telemetry / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js), sweep the fleet for other hosts resolving the domain, and audit any downstream package pinning 1.20.21.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl =~ "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name =~ "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode = ResultCodeName, ResolvedIPs = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 payload file dropped on disk AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the tainted SDK landing in node_modules on developer workstations, build agents, or servers via the distinctive payload filenames (key-derivation-telemetry.ts/.js, dist/esm/accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) and the two published SHA256 hashes. These artifacts do not exist in the clean SDK, making on-disk presence unambiguous evidence of the compromised 1.20.21 release. Rationale: Uses the payload filenames from Stage 2 (key-derivation-telemetry.ts and compiled dist/esm/accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) plus the two article-published SHA256 hashes — none of which exist in the clean 1.20.23 build — so any hit is a direct indicator of the tainted release rather than a behavioural heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/injective-labs-github-compromise-pushes.html • https://slowmist.medium.com/threat-intelligence-injective-sdk-compromised-crypto-wallet-private-keys-stolen-0b8f06bf37ad
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security tooling (Socket, Snyk, Ox Security) storing a quarantined/sample copy of the malicious file for analysis
  • A malware analyst manually saving the IOC file to a case folder
  • Backup or artifact-cache restore replaying an old node_modules tree containing 1.20.21
  • An unrelated project coincidentally shipping a benign file named key-derivation-telemetry.js (hash mismatch distinguishes it)
Suppression filter
// drop AV/EDR quarantine and analyst sample copies
| where FolderPath !contains "Quarantine" and FolderPath !contains "\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\samples"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FolderPath sits under node_modules/@injectivelabs and check whether SHA256 matches a published hash; identify the writing process (npm/pnpm/yarn/node) and the account. 2) Contain: quarantine/remove the tainted package, force reinstall of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.23+ with a fresh lockfile, and clear npm/pnpm caches on the host and shared CI cache. 3) Hunt: rotate every wallet seed/private key any app on that host derived while 1.20.21 was resident, then sweep the fleet and build agents for the same filenames/hashes and for outbound contact to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("key-derivation-telemetry.ts","key-derivation-telemetry.js","accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
    or SHA256 in ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0","9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("key-derivation-telemetry.ts","key-derivation-telemetry.js","accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

ImFileEvent

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed · [LLM] Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) · [LLM] TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) · [LLM] Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) · [LLM] CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain)
Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the hardcoded self-propagating payload files the Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon npm worm drops during a malicious package preinstall, matched by exact filename and known SHA256. The article cites Sha1-Hulud dumping harvested credentials into public GitHub repos as the exfiltration destination it warns about; this catches the worm at the execution stage before that exfil happens. Rationale: Uses the exact worm payload filenames (setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) and four published SHA256 hashes from Datadog/Microsoft analyses of Sha1-Hulud 2.0 — the campaign the article names as the archetype of GitHub-hosted secret exfiltration. Filename+hash makes this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a captured Sha1-Hulud sample in a sandbox VONM
  • Threat-intel/malware-repo mirror syncing sample files to a scanning host
  • EDR test/purple-team exercise seeding the named hashes
  • A benign project legitimately shipping a file literally named setup_bun.js (rare; hash filter avoids this)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\MalwareSamples\\","\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA256 matches a known worm hash and identify the InitiatingProcess (should be node/npm/bun preinstall). Pull the parent package name and package.json to find the poisoned dependency. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner, revoke any npm/GitHub/cloud tokens present on it, and freeze the developer's npm publish rights. Step 3 (hunt): Search the org for the same hashes and for any public GitHub repos with description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.'; rotate every secret reachable from the affected build.

| where FileName in~ ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
   or SHA256 in~ ("a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a","62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0","cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd","f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
   or TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a","62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0","cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd","f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a JavaScript package-manager process (node, npm, bun, yarn, pnpm) reaching the cloud instance-metadata service (169.254.169.254 or metadata.google.internal) — the multi-cloud credential-harvest step of the Sha1-Hulud worm. This is the 'secret theft that never touches github.com' the article says public monitoring cannot see. Rationale: Combines the concrete IMDS endpoints (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal) documented by Datadog/Unit42 with the JS package-manager parent context that distinguishes worm harvesting from a legitimate cloud SDK call. Pins the abuse to the install-time process rather than any app. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js application running on an EC2/GCE instance that legitimately queries IMDS via the AWS/GCP SDK
  • Serverless/build tooling (e.g. serverless-framework, terraform-node wrappers) resolving instance credentials
  • Cloud-native CI agents written in Node fetching a metadata-scoped token for artifact upload
  • IMDSv2 token-refresh loops from a long-running node service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall","ci","npx") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node_modules"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the node/bun process was part of an npm/yarn install lifecycle (check parent chain and recent package.json changes) versus a steady-state application. Install-time IMDS access is the true positive. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the instance role's temporary credentials, quarantine the runner/host, and enforce IMDSv2 hop-limit=1 to block the container reach. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host for setup_bun.js/bun_environment.js, trufflehog execution, and any subsequent api.github.com repo creation; rotate cloud keys the role could reach.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the TruffleHog secret-discovery binary launched as a child of a JavaScript package manager or a shell inside an install script — the on-disk credential-sweep stage of the Sha1-Hulud worm. Distinct from sanctioned CI secret-scanning because the parent is node/npm/bun rather than a dedicated scanner job. Rationale: TruffleHog execution parented by node/bun/npm is the documented Sha1-Hulud secret-discovery step (Datadog/Wiz). The parent-process predicate separates worm-driven scans from an intentional trufflehog CI stage, keeping fidelity up. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A CI pipeline that legitimately runs trufflehog as a pre-commit/secret-scan step invoked from an npm script
  • Developer running `npx trufflehog` manually to audit a repo
  • Security tooling wrappers that shell out to trufflehog from a Node orchestrator
  • pre-commit framework invoking trufflehog via a node hook
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pre-commit","secret-scan","security-scan","gitleaks-trufflehog-step"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm trufflehog was not a sanctioned pipeline step — inspect the initiating package.json script and whether the run coincides with an npm install rather than a scan job. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner and revoke tokens; if part of a build, halt the pipeline and quarantine produced artifacts. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with IMDS access, bun payload files, and outbound api.github.com repo creation on the same host; rotate any secrets trufflehog could have read.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","npm.cmd","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "trufflehog" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm registering an attacker-controlled self-hosted GitHub Actions runner — identified by the runner name SHA1HULUD, the $HOME/.dev-env install directory, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, and the actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0 download. This is the worm turning GitHub into a persistence/C2 channel, exactly the github.com-as-infrastructure abuse the article describes. Rationale: Pins on four hard, campaign-unique strings from Datadog's Sha1-Hulud 2.0 analysis (runner name SHA1HULUD, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, ~/.dev-env, actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0). These do not appear in legitimate runner setups, giving alerting-grade fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1543 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An org that coincidentally uses a self-hosted runner directory named .dev-env (unlikely, and runner-name string still filters it)
  • Admin legitimately setting RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1 in a container runner build (would lack the SHA1HULUD name)
  • Runner version 2.330.0 downloaded during a legitimate GitHub-hosted runner upgrade (string paired with the other markers reduces this)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the runner registration name is SHA1HULUD or the install path is $HOME/.dev-env; check which GitHub org/repo the runner registered against. Step 2 (contain): Remove the runner from GitHub org settings, kill the runner process, revoke the PAT/GITHUB_TOKEN it used, and isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Search GitHub audit logs for self-hosted runner additions and for workflows triggered `on: discussion` with a `runs-on: self-hosted` job echoing github.event.discussion.body; enumerate other hosts with .dev-env.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm's destructive fallback that fires when it cannot authenticate/propagate: on Windows `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%` plus `cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, and on Linux `find $HOME ... | xargs shred -uvz`. High-impact, low-frequency behaviour that turns a supply-chain compromise into data destruction. Rationale: Encodes the exact destructive commands Datadog documented for Sha1-Hulud's failure path (`cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%*`, `find $HOME ... shred -uvz`). cipher /W over a user profile and shred over $HOME are near-zero in normal ops, making impact-stage alerting reliable. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/GPO running `cipher /W:` to wipe free space during decommissioning (usually not scoped to %USERPROFILE% and not spawned by node)
  • Backup or forensics tooling using shred for secure deletion of scratch data
  • A cleanup script using recursive del on a temp path (USERPROFILE token filter reduces this)
  • Disk-sanitisation compliance jobs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","sh","bash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or FileName =~ "cipher.exe"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the parent process — a wipe parented by node/bun/sh during an npm install is the true positive; capture the exact target path. Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate the host from the network to stop further destruction and preserve volume shadow copies/backups; snapshot the disk. Step 3 (hunt): Confirm the Sha1-Hulud chain (bun payloads, trufflehog, IMDS, SHA1HULUD runner) on the host and across the fleet; initiate restore-from-backup and org-wide secret rotation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "cipher.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "cipher.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Sha1-Hulud Destructive Wiper Fallback

CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a package-manager process reaching cloud IMDS with the same host contacting api.github.com/github.com within 30 minutes — the Sha1-Hulud pattern of harvesting cloud secrets then pushing them into a newly created public GitHub repo. This directly targets the 'close the exfiltration gap' thesis of the article: catching secrets leaving CI toward github.com, not after they surface. Rationale: Chains the two documented Sha1-Hulud network behaviours (IMDS credential harvest → push to a new github.com repo) on the same host within a tight window, which is far more specific than either signal alone and maps precisely to the article's exfiltration-to-github concern. Time-window correlation makes it a hunt, not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node app on a cloud VM that reads IMDS and also pushes to GitHub (e.g. a release bot / GitOps agent) within the window
  • CI runner that legitimately fetches instance credentials then interacts with the GitHub API for status checks
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation touching both IMDS and github.com
  • Container build that queries metadata for a token and pushes an image manifest referencing github.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall") or RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the github.com interaction — was a NEW repo created (check GitHub audit log for repo.create with an 18-char hex name or description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.')? Confirm the IMDS call was install-time. Step 2 (contain): Delete the attacker repo, revoke the developer's GitHub token and the instance role credentials, and isolate the host/runner. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for bun payload files, trufflehog, and the SHA1HULUD runner on the host; enumerate all public repos org-wide matching the campaign description and rotate every exposed secret.

Compromised jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Release Drops Rust Infostealer During Install

The Hacker News
2026-07-11 14 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The jscrambler npm package was compromised, and simply installing its&nbsp;8.14.0&nbsp;release runs an infostealer on your machine. Published on July 11, 2026, the malicious version carries a&nbsp;preinstall&nbsp;hook that drops and executes a native binary, one build each for Windows, macOS, and Linux. Socket flagged the release&nbsp;six minutes after it was published. If you or one of your

jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Package Installation AIDelivery High
Hunts for installation of the compromised jscrambler CLI npm package (8.14.0 and the sibling malicious versions 8.16.0/8.17.0/8.18.0/8.20.0 tied to the same actor) via npm/pnpm/yarn command lines on developer and CI hosts. Article-specific because it pins the exact package name and poisoned version window rather than generic npm abuse. Rationale: Anchors on the exact package name 'jscrambler' plus the poisoned version set from the article (8.14.0) enriched with the sibling malicious versions Socket attributed to the same actor. Version-pinned package name in an install command is very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A dependency-audit or SCA tool that echoes 'jscrambler@8.14.0' in its scan output command line
  • A remediation script explicitly uninstalling/overriding jscrambler@8.14.0 (npm uninstall / npm ls output)
  • A CI lockfile-pinning job that references the version string while forcing an upgrade to 8.15.0
  • A developer reproducing the incident in an isolated sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("uninstall","npm ls","npm audit","remove"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the command was an install (npm install/ci/add) not an uninstall/audit, and check whether the host is a build agent or developer laptop with access to cloud keys. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node.exe child processes, and remove jscrambler@8.14.0 from lockfiles/caches; pin to 8.13.0 or 8.15.0. 3) Hunt: on any confirmed install, treat all reachable secrets as stolen — rotate AWS/Azure/GCP keys, npm/GitHub tokens, and AI-tool/MCP API keys; pivot to UC2/UC3 to find the dropped binary and C2 callbacks.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe") or FileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jscrambler" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("8.14.0","8.16.0","8.17.0","8.18.0","8.20.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rust Infostealer Binary Execution from npm Post-Install Hook AIInstallation High
Detects the setup.js preinstall loader (run by node.exe/npm) writing a hidden, randomly-named native binary into the system temp directory and executing it detached. Matches on the three published payload hashes and on the node→temp-hidden-executable parent/child chain specific to this campaign. Rationale: Uses the three published decompressed payload SHA-256 values plus the article's described chain (setup.js under node writes a hidden .{random}/.{random}.exe into temp and launches it detached). Hash match is deterministic; the behavioral clause catches recompiled variants. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate node-gyp / native-addon builds that write and run compiled binaries from temp during install
  • Electron or Puppeteer post-install steps that unpack helper binaries into temp
  • Test frameworks that spawn short-lived helper executables from a temp workspace
  • A developer's own build tool that emits dot-prefixed cache files in temp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","electron-builder") and SHA256 !in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: if a hash matches, this is confirmed malware — no further validation needed; for the behavioral hit, inspect the temp file name/signature and whether it was launched detached with hidden output. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the temp process tree, and capture the binary for the DFIR queue before AV quarantine removes it. 3) Hunt: pivot on the process ID into UC3 (C2 to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79), UC4 (credential file access), and UC5 (persistence) on the same host and across all CI agents that pulled jscrambler in the July 11+ window.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe") and FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/") and FileName startswith ".")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
   or (ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/"))

IronWorm C2 beacon to hardcoded jscrambler stealer IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host reaching the two hard-coded attacker C2 IP addresses (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) that StepSecurity observed the dropped jscrambler stealer contacting over TLS. Pure network-IOC pivot; independent of process telemetry so it catches the stealer even if EDR missed the drop. Rationale: Uses the two direct attacker C2 IPs StepSecurity published — the first network indicators for the campaign, confirmed across multiple write-ups. Static malicious IPs have essentially no legitimate business use. cloudwatch_query left empty: this is endpoint/firewall egress telemetry that does not live in CloudTrail, and VPC Flow fields fall outside the CloudTrail whitelist. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel enrichment or sandbox appliance deliberately connecting to the IOC IPs for analysis
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a lab that shares the corporate egress
  • Shared cloud-provider IP reuse if the attacker infra is later reassigned (Hetzner/OVH ranges)
  • A vulnerability scanner probing the IPs as part of external attack-surface testing
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the host — if it maps to a temp-dropped hidden binary or node.exe child, escalate to confirmed stealer C2. 2) Contain: block 37.27.122.124 and 57.128.246.79 at the perimeter/EDR, isolate the source host, and snapshot memory. 3) Hunt: sweep all egress logs for these IPs and Tor bootstrap traffic (check.torproject.org / archive.torproject.org) from build agents; correlate to UC1 installs and rotate every secret reachable from that host.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Credential/Browser Data Theft Post-npm Install AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a hidden temp-directory process (the dropped Rust stealer) touching the specific secret stores the article enumerates: AWS/Azure/GCP credentials, .ssh keys, Chrome/Edge user data, Bitwarden/MetaMask/Exodus/Phantom wallets, and AI-coding-tool configs (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Zed) that hold API keys and MCP credentials. Rationale: Pairs the article's exact target list (AWS/Azure/GCP, .ssh, Chrome/Edge, Bitwarden, MetaMask/Exodus/Phantom, and the newer AI-tool configs for Claude/Cursor/Windsurf/VS Code/Zed) with the initiating process being the hidden temp-dropped binary — the two together are far more specific than any single credential-store access. datadog_query empty: Sysmon does not emit reliable file-read events (EID 11 is create-only), so this read-centric detection cannot be faithfully expressed on Datadog Windows telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1552.001 T1005

  • A browser or password-manager updater accessing its own User Data directory
  • A legitimate AI coding assistant (Cursor/Windsurf) reading its own config from an installer staged in temp
  • Endpoint AV scanning the same secret directories

| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("aws.exe","az.exe","gcloud","bitwarden","chrome.exe","msedge.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files", "/usr/bin/", "/opt/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the acting process is the hidden temp binary (dot-prefixed, random name) and not a signed vendor updater; check how many distinct secret stores it touched in the window. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the binary; assume every accessed store is compromised. 3) Hunt: rotate the specific secrets touched — cloud keys, SSH keys, browser sessions, Bitwarden vault, and AI-tool/MCP API keys — then sweep other hosts that installed jscrambler for the same acting-process pattern.

Persistence written by temp-dropped binary (hidden sched task / macOS LaunchAgent) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the stealer wiring in reboot persistence: a hidden Windows scheduled task set to relaunch every minute (schtasks /create ... minute) spawned from a temp-directory process, or a macOS LaunchAgent plist written into ~/Library/LaunchAgents by a process running from /tmp or /var/folders. Rationale: Anchors on the article's precise persistence detail — a hidden scheduled task set to relaunch every minute, and a macOS LaunchAgent reloading on login — combined with the parent being the temp-dropped binary. The Sentinel query now keys on 4688 NewProcessName + CommandLine instead of the non-existent TaskName column. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers creating per-minute health-check tasks from a temp-extracted setup binary
  • Monitoring agents (RMM tools) registering frequent scheduled tasks during deployment
  • macOS app installers dropping a LaunchAgent plist from a staged installer in /var/folders
  • An admin script creating a recurring task while logged in from an elevated temp-run tool
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentProcessName has_any ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("Adobe","Google","Microsoft"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the task action/target binary (schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml) or the LaunchAgent plist contents — a target pointing to a hidden temp file is confirmed malicious. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task / remove the LaunchAgent plist, kill the referenced binary, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search all jscrambler-affected hosts for per-minute tasks and unfamiliar ~/Library/LaunchAgents plists created since July 11, and correlate the task target hash against the UC2 payload hashes.
union

  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "minute" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Artifact = ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath),
 (DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and FileName endswith ".plist" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Artifact = FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "minute"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

jscrambler Package Tampering Artifact Detection AIDelivery Medium
Detects the tell-tale supply-chain artifacts of the compromise: the added dist/setup.js loader and dist/intro.js (a ~7.8MB binary container despite the .js name) appearing under node_modules/jscrambler, matched by the two published file hashes or by path+filename. These files exist in the npm tarball but nowhere in jscrambler's public source. Rationale: Uses the two published SHA-256 hashes for dist/setup.js and dist/intro.js plus the exact path/filename pattern (node_modules/jscrambler/dist). Multiple analysts (StepSecurity, SafeDep, Socket) confirmed these files exist in the tarball but not in the public repo, making their presence on disk high-fidelity supply-chain evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated package or project that legitimately ships files named setup.js/intro.js in a directory containing 'jscrambler' in its path
  • A security researcher storing the extracted malicious files in a case folder path containing 'jscrambler'
  • A backup/restore operation replaying the tarball into a quarantined node_modules for analysis
  • A vendored copy of a clean older jscrambler release that happens to include a setup.js
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\case\\", "\\quarantine\\", "\\samples\\", "/analysis/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the on-disk setup.js/intro.js and compare to the published values; a match plus a ~7.8MB intro.js confirms the tampered package. 2) Contain: remove the node_modules/jscrambler tree and the lockfile pin, isolate the host if the preinstall hook already ran, and rebuild from a clean 8.13.0/8.15.0. 3) Hunt: search artifact registries, container images, and CI caches for these two hashes, then pivot to UC2/UC3 on any host where the files were present to confirm whether the payload executed.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60","a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86")
   or (FolderPath has "jscrambler" and FileName in~ ("setup.js","intro.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60","a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86")
   or (TargetFilePath has "jscrambler" and TargetFileName in~ ("setup.js","intro.js"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

DeviceFileEvents

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
