XQUIC/Tengine HTTP/3 worker abort from QPACK ring-buffer overflow (XRING) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the server-side crash signature of the XRING flaw: a Tengine/nginx worker embedding Alibaba's XQUIC library dies with a glibc _FORTIFY_SOURCE 'buffer overflow detected' abort (SIGABRT/6) or an out-of-bounds SIGSEGV (11) after ~260 bytes of spec-compliant QPACK encoder-stream traffic. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact processes (xquic/tengine/nginx) and the fortify-abort behaviour FoxIO reproduced on Ubuntu 26.04. Rationale: Anchors on FoxIO's stated crash mechanism (glibc _FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 abort on Ubuntu 26.04) plus the exact XQUIC-embedding processes named in the article (Tengine/nginx/xquic). The 'buffer overflow detected' glibc string and nginx 'worker process N exited on signal 6/11' master-log lines are the only reliable observable because the QPACK trigger traffic is spec-compliant and rides an encrypted QUIC stream. Cross-checked FoxIO blog, the public XRING PoC repo, and THN. Cross-checked against: • https://foxio.io/blog/xring-crashing-xquic-with-spec-compliant-qpack-instructions • https://github.com/FoxIO-LLC/xring-poc • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-xring-flaw-in-xquic-lets.html • https://threat-modeling.com/xring-xquic-unpatched-flaw-crash-http3-servers/
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1499
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine unrelated memory-safety bug in a third-party nginx/tengine module (e.g. luajit, brotli, custom C module) triggering the same fortify abort
  • Lab or QA hosts running ASAN/debug builds during vulnerability testing that legitimately print overflow diagnostics
  • OOM-killer terminating a worker (signal 9) - excluded by the signal 6/11 filter but analysts may still see nearby noise
  • Administrator issuing 'nginx -s reload' recycling workers (clean exit, not 'exited on signal') - excluded by the signal-exit pattern
  • OpenSSL/QUIC stack crash from an unrelated malformed-packet CVE rather than XRING
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "signal 9" and SyslogMessage !has "signal 15" and SyslogMessage !has "gracefully shutting down" and Computer !has "lab" and Computer !has "test"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full worker error-log context around the abort - confirm the process is Tengine/nginx built with XQUIC and that HTTP/3 (UDP 443) is enabled with a non-zero SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY; check whether the crash repeats (XRING is a repeatable, low-byte remote crash). 2) Contain: apply the vendor workaround now - set SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY to 0 to disable the QPACK dynamic table, or disable HTTP/3 (listen ... quic) on the affected vhost until a fixed XQUIC release ships. 3) Hunt: correlate the crash timestamp with UDP/443 QUIC source IPs (firewall/LB logs) to identify the client(s) driving the resize, pivot on that IP across all internet-facing HTTP/3 servers, and check for crash-loop bursts (see companion crash-loop UC).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ProcessName has_any ("nginx","tengine","xquic") or SyslogMessage has_any ("nginx","tengine","xquic")
| where SyslogMessage has "buffer overflow detected"
   or SyslogMessage matches regex @"worker process \d+ exited on signal (6|11)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: XQUIC/Tengine HTTP-3 Worker Crash via QPACK Ring-Buffer Overflow (XRING)
id: 8f2c9d41-7a3e-4b6f-9c21-5d0e1a7b3f88
status: experimental
description: Detects the server-side crash signature of the XRING XQUIC QPACK dynamic-table ring-buffer overflow - a Tengine/nginx worker aborting with a glibc buffer-overflow fortify message or exiting on SIGABRT(6)/SIGSEGV(11).
references:
  - https://foxio.io/blog/xring-crashing-xquic-with-spec-compliant-qpack-instructions
  - https://github.com/FoxIO-LLC/xring-poc
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-xring-flaw-in-xquic-lets.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1499.004
logsource:
  product: linux
  service: syslog
detection:
  selection_proc:
    - 'nginx'
    - 'tengine'
    - 'xquic'
  selection_crash:
    - 'buffer overflow detected'
    - 'exited on signal 6'
    - 'exited on signal 11'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_crash
falsepositives:
  - Unrelated memory-safety bug in a third-party nginx module
  - Lab/ASAN debug builds during vulnerability testing
level: high
source:linux.syslog (@process.name:(nginx OR tengine OR xquic) OR nginx OR tengine OR xquic) ("buffer overflow detected" OR "exited on signal 6" OR "exited on signal 11")
WEB
index=* (sourcetype="nginx:plus:error" OR sourcetype=nginx_error OR sourcetype=syslog OR source="/var/log/nginx/error.log" OR source="/var/log/tengine/error.log") (nginx OR tengine OR xquic) ("buffer overflow detected" OR ("worker process" AND ("exited on signal 6" OR "exited on signal 11"))) | rex "worker process (?<worker_pid>\d+) exited on signal (?<signal>\d+)" | table _time host worker_pid signal _raw | sort - _time
Tengine/nginx HTTP/3 worker crash-loop burst (XRING remote DoS) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts when a Tengine/nginx master respawns HTTP/3 workers abnormally fast - the availability symptom of repeated XRING crashes, where a remote client sends short bursts of legal QPACK traffic that repeatedly kill and force respawn of worker processes. Threshold-based, so it catches sustained exploitation even when individual crash strings are missed. Rationale: Models the article's core claim - 'a short burst of completely legal traffic takes the server process down' - as its observable operational consequence: rapid worker respawn/crash cycling on the affected Tengine/nginx+XQUIC hosts. Uses only process-create telemetry (available on Defender-Linux, FDR, CIM, and syslog) so it survives even when the glibc crash string isn't captured. Threshold (>10 respawns / >5 crashes per 5 min) separates a crash storm from occasional reloads. Cross-checked against: • https://foxio.io/blog/xring-crashing-xquic-with-spec-compliant-qpack-instructions • https://github.com/FoxIO-LLC/xring-poc • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-xring-flaw-in-xquic-lets.html
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1499
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate config reloads/rotations under automation (Ansible, cert renewal) recycling workers in bursts
  • Autoscaling or blue/green deploys restarting the web tier repeatedly in a short window
  • An unrelated crashing nginx module causing a respawn loop independent of HTTP/3
  • OOM pressure on a memory-starved host cycling workers (signal 9) - excluded by the signal 6/11 filter in the syslog variant
  • Health-check or load-test tooling hammering the server and triggering non-XRING restarts
Suppression filter
| where SampleCmd !has "-s reload" and SampleCmd !has "-t" and DeviceName !has "canary" and DeviceName !has "staging"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the respawning binary is HTTP/3-enabled Tengine/nginx with XQUIC, and check whether the syslog variant shows signal 6/11 exits (crash) vs clean reloads; correlate the 5-min bucket with deploy/automation change tickets to rule out benign restarts. 2) Contain: if crashes are confirmed and no change window explains them, disable HTTP/3 or set SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY=0 on the vhost and, if a single source IP dominates, block it at the edge/LB for UDP 443. 3) Hunt: enumerate all internet-facing hosts running XQUIC/Tengine (see exposure UC), review LB/QUIC connection logs for the source IP(s) driving the resize, and check for the same respawn burst across the fleet indicating a targeted sweep.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where FileName in~ ("nginx","tengine")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nginx","tengine")   // master respawning a worker after a crash
| summarize RespawnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine)
          by DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where RespawnCount > 10   // >10 worker respawns / 5 min = crash loop; steady-state respawns ~= worker count and reloads are rare
| order by RespawnCount desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ProcessName has_any ("nginx","tengine") or SyslogMessage has_any ("nginx","tengine")
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"worker process \d+ exited on signal (6|11)"
| summarize Crashes = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleMsg = any(SyslogMessage)
          by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Crashes > 5   // >5 abnormal worker exits / 5 min indicates repeated XRING crash attempts
| order by Crashes desc
source:linux.syslog (@process.name:(nginx OR tengine) OR nginx OR tengine) ("exited on signal 6" OR "exited on signal 11")
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(nginx|tengine)$/i ParentBaseFileName=/(nginx|tengine)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(as=respawns))
| respawns > 10
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("nginx","tengine") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("nginx","tengine")) by Processes.dest, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count > 10 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("nginx","tengine") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("nginx","tengine")) by Processes.dest, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count > 10 | sort - count
Exposure hunt: internet-facing hosts running XQUIC/Tengine (<=v1.9.4) with HTTP/3 AIReconnaissance Medium
Proactive attack-surface hunt for assets exposed to XRING: every XQUIC release through v1.9.4 is affected and there is no fix or CVE, so any internet-facing host running Tengine or an XQUIC-linked server with HTTP/3 and the default QPACK dynamic table is vulnerable. Surfaces the inventory an operator needs to apply the SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY=0 / disable-HTTP-3 workaround. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete affected-software facts (Alibaba XQUIC through v1.9.4, embedded in Tengine, no fix/CVE) to enumerate exposed assets rather than inventing on-wire probe signatures the encrypted QPACK stream would defeat. It directly operationalises the article's own mitigation guidance by finding where to apply it. Medium confidence because XQUIC as a linked library may not always appear in software inventory - the process-based Falcon/CIM variants catch running Tengine/nginx as a fallback. Cross-checked against: • https://foxio.io/blog/xring-crashing-xquic-with-spec-compliant-qpack-instructions • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-xring-flaw-in-xquic-lets.html
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tengine/nginx instances that do NOT serve HTTP/3 (no 'listen ... quic' / UDP 443) - present in inventory but not actually exposed to XRING
  • Internal-only Tengine instances (not internet-facing) that carry lower risk
  • Hosts already mitigated with SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY=0 that still show the software present
  • nginx builds that are NOT linked against XQUIC (mainline nginx without the Alibaba QUIC library) matched by the process-name fallback
  • Reverse proxies terminating HTTP/3 upstream where the vulnerable component sits elsewhere in the chain
Suppression filter
| where IsInternetFacing == true or isempty(IsInternetFacing)
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm HTTP/3 is actually enabled (UDP 443 listener / Alt-Svc h3 advertisement) and that the build links XQUIC through v1.9.4; prioritise IsInternetFacing==true assets, especially CDN/edge and consumer-facing sites. 2) Contain: on confirmed-exposed hosts set SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY to 0 (disables the QPACK dynamic table) or disable HTTP/3 entirely until a fixed XQUIC release ships. 3) Hunt: feed the confirmed host list into the two crash-detection UCs for continuous monitoring, and scan the perimeter for any additional UDP/443 QUIC listeners not yet in the asset inventory.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has_any ("xquic","tengine")
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId
  ) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, SoftwareName asc
// every version through v1.9.4 is affected and there is no fixed release - treat any hit as exposed
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(tengine OR nginx OR xquic)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(tengine|nginx|xquic)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("tengine","nginx") by Processes.dest, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | stats values(process_name) as servers values(process_path) as paths count by dest | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("tengine","nginx") by Processes.dest, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | stats values(process_name) as servers values(process_path) as paths count by dest | sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed Hacker Server Reveals WP-SHELLSTORM Backdooring Thousands of WordPress Sites

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 18 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A cybercrime crew left one of its own servers wide open on the internet for three weeks, and it exposed the operation's inner workings: the hacking tools, the activity logs, and target lists naming more than 1.4 million websites. Far fewer were actually broken into, but the exposed files showed researchers how a mass site-hacking operation runs from the inside. The operation, now tracked as

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Nacos CVE-2021-29441 auth bypass via spoofed 'Nacos-Server' User-Agent from external IP · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] WP-SHELLSTORM webshell drop: PHP file written into wp-content/uploads or cache by web-server process · [LLM] VShell in-memory backdoor masquerading as [kworker/N:M] kernel thread · [LLM] WP-SHELLSTORM primary webshell 'down.php' written under wp-content · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to WP-SHELLSTORM operator infrastructure (137.175.93.126 / 43.108.17.80 / xxooonline.eu.cc) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] WordPress web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx) spawning shell, downloader or recon binary · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Nacos CVE-2021-29441 auth bypass via spoofed 'Nacos-Server' User-Agent from external IP AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the earlier WP-SHELLSTORM corporate-credential campaign step: the crew abused Nacos CVE-2021-29441 by faking the User-Agent header 'Nacos-Server' to skip authentication and dump config (AWS/Alibaba/Oracle/Tencent/DigitalOcean keys, DB passwords, Alipay RSA keys). Fires on external requests to /nacos/ endpoints carrying that magic User-Agent. Rationale: Article names Nacos CVE-2021-29441 and the 'fake a single web header' bypass; cross-checked against GitHub Security Lab GHSL-2020-325 and NVD which confirm the magic User-Agent is literally 'Nacos-Server'. External-source filter removes the only clean FP (intra-cluster peer sync). Cross-checked against: • https://securitylab.github.com/advisories/GHSL-2020-325_326-nacos/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-29441 • https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Nacos cluster peer-to-peer sync (uses Nacos-Server UA but on private/internal IPs)
  • Internal service registration/health-check traffic to the config server
  • Load balancer or APM health probes reaching /nacos/ health endpoints
  • Security scanners (internal Nessus/Qualys) replaying the CVE-2021-29441 check
Suppression filter
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all /nacos/ requests from the flagged SourceIP over the last 30d; confirm the UA is 'Nacos-Server' and the requests hit /nacos/v1/cs/configs, /nacos/v1/auth/users, or config export paths from an external IP. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, take the Nacos instance off the public internet, set nacos.core.auth.enabled=true and upgrade to >=2.2.1. 3) Hunt: assume config was read - rotate EVERY credential stored in Nacos (AWS/Alibaba/Oracle/Tencent/DigitalOcean keys, DB passwords, Alipay RSA private keys), then hunt those keys' usage in cloud CloudTrail/audit logs for attacker reuse.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestClientApplication =~ "Nacos-Server"
| where RequestURL has "/nacos/"
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false   // legit intra-cluster peer sync legitimately uses this UA on private IPs
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WP-SHELLSTORM webshell drop: PHP file written into wp-content/uploads or cache by web-server process AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the webshell-plant step of the mass backdoor campaign. Exploits (Breeze CVE-2026-3844, JCE, file-manager bugs) write a PHP payload into upload/cache directories that should never contain executable PHP. Flags .php files created under /wp-content/uploads/ or /wp-content/cache/ (incl. Breeze cache dirs) by php-fpm/apache/nginx. Rationale: Breeze CVE-2026-3844's gravatar-local-hosting write primitive and the campaign's upload-based webshell delivery both land PHP in uploads/cache dirs that legitimately never hold executable PHP; scoping to those dirs + web-server writer keeps it high-signal without a hash we don't have. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/ • https://www.esecurityplanet.com/threats/wp-shellstorm-exposed-hackers-backdoored-thousands-of-wordpress-websites/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Caching/optimization plugins (WP Rocket, W3 Total Cache) legitimately writing .php cache objects under wp-content/cache
  • Backup/migration plugins staging PHP into uploads during export
  • A plugin auto-update unpacking into wp-content/plugins/breeze
  • Developer manually copying a maintenance script into uploads
  • Object-cache drop-ins written during plugin install
Suppression filter
| where not (TargetFilePath has "/wp-content/cache/" and ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php") and TargetFileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{16,}\.php$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the created .php file - webshells show heavy obfuscation (base64_decode/gzinflate/eval, single-letter vars) and a filename like down.php; confirm the writing process and the HTTP request that immediately preceded it in web logs. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, take the vhost into maintenance mode, and reset the site's admin + DB credentials. 3) Hunt: sweep the whole docroot for sibling PHP shells, pivot on the writer PID for child shells and outbound connections to the campaign C2, and check whether the Breeze 'Host Files Locally - Gravatars' setting is enabled.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/wp-content/uploads/", "/wp-content/cache/", "/wp-content/plugins/breeze/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx","sh","bash","curl","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/wp-content/uploads/", "/wp-content/cache/", "/wp-content/plugins/breeze/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx) spawning shell, downloader or recon binary AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts webshell command execution: down.php (BestShell-derived) can run commands, open reverse shells, scan the network and enumerate installed security software. Detects a web-server/PHP parent spawning sh/bash/curl/wget/nc or recon tools (whoami/id/uname), which a healthy PHP app almost never does. Rationale: Article states the webshell can run commands, open reverse shells, scan the network and check installed security software - all of which surface as a web-server parent spawning shells/downloaders/recon tools, a pairing (parent web daemon + shell child) that is near-zero in healthy PHP apps. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/exposed-hacker-server-reveals-wp.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003 T1046
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WP-Cron or a plugin legitimately shelling out to ImageMagick/ffmpeg/pdftk for media processing
  • Backup plugins invoking mysqldump/tar via shell_exec
  • A monitoring agent embedded in the app calling curl for outbound webhooks
  • WooCommerce/plugin calling wget to fetch remote assets
  • Deployment tooling running as the web user during a release window
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/", "bash -i", "-e /bin", "nc -e", "whoami", "uname -a", "/etc/passwd") or not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("api.", "cdn.", "webhook"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full child ProcessCommandLine - reverse-shell markers (/dev/tcp/, bash -i, nc -e), network scans or security-software enumeration confirm webshell use over benign plugin exec. 2) Contain: kill the child + parent PHP worker, isolate the host, and block any C2 IP/domain the child reached. 3) Hunt: from the same host, pull the writing web request in access logs, sweep the docroot for the dropped shell (down.php and siblings), and check for the VShell [kworker] masquerade and outbound connections to campaign infrastructure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","whoami","id","uname")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","whoami","id","uname")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VShell in-memory backdoor masquerading as [kworker/N:M] kernel thread AIInstallation High
Detects the crew's own remote-access implant: SNOWLIGHT drops VShell, which runs fileless (memfd_create/fexecve) and renames its process to [kworker/0:2] to blend with genuine kernel threads. A userland process whose name mimics a kthread but has a real image/argv is a high-fidelity UNC5174-linked signal. Rationale: Article explicitly states VShell 'disguises its process name as [kworker/0:2] to blend in with the kernel threads'; Sysdig/THN/Wiz confirm the memfd_create+fexecve fileless exec under a kworker name is a signature UNC5174 technique. Genuine kthreads never appear in EDR process-create with an on-disk image, making this near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2025/04/chinese-hackers-target-linux-systems.html • https://threats.wiz.io/all-incidents/unc5174-linux-espionage-campaign • https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1620 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EDR/Sysmon-for-Linux occasionally surfacing a genuine kernel worker during agent startup (rare, no image hash)
  • A sysadmin naming a test binary 'kworker' out of curiosity
  • Container runtimes emitting synthetic process names during namespace setup
  • Kernel-thread accounting glitches in older auditd builds
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process has a real executable/memfd backing and non-empty argv (genuine kthreads do not) and inspect ParentProcessName - a web/dropper parent is damning. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory (fileless payload lives only in RAM), and kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host's outbound connections for VShell C2, look for the SNOWLIGHT dropper and memfd_create/fexecve syscall activity, and correlate to any preceding webshell command execution on the same box.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\[kworker/[0-9]+:[0-9]+\]" or FileName matches regex @"^\[kworker"
| where isnotempty(SHA256) or FolderPath has "memfd"   // real kthreads have no on-disk image; memfd = fileless exec
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"\[kworker/" or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\[kworker/[0-9]+:[0-9]+\]"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection to WP-SHELLSTORM operator infrastructure (137.175.93.126 / 43.108.17.80 / xxooonline.eu.cc) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host reaching the crew's exposed tooling/C2 infrastructure: the open-directory VPS 137.175.93.126, the secondary IP 43.108.17.80, or the domain xs.xxooonline.eu.cc. A hit means either a compromised web server calling home or an internal host pulling attacker tooling. Rationale: These are the concrete network IOCs the article and SOCRadar tie to the operation - 137.175.93.126 is the exposed operator VPS, plus the secondary IP and xs.xxooonline.eu.cc domain; direct-match IOCs warrant alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/exposed-hacker-server-reveals-wp.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or your own threat-intel team deliberately visiting the exposed server (as the Taiwan IP that pulled 42,000 tool downloads did)
  • A sandbox/detonation VM resolving the domain during analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment services fetching the IOC for reputation scoring
  • A shared-hosting neighbor IP reuse after the VPS is reclaimed (validate the IP is still attributed before high-sev escalation)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome","msedge","firefox","curl") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection - a web-server/PHP process or a [kworker] masquerade confirms compromise vs. a browser/TI-tool which is likely benign research. 2) Contain: block all three IOCs at the perimeter, isolate the calling host, and snapshot it. 3) Hunt: on the calling host, look for the down.php webshell, PHP-spawned shells, and the SNOWLIGHT/VShell chain; expand the IOC block to any newly-observed sibling infrastructure from passive DNS on xxooonline.eu.cc.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("137.175.93.126", "43.108.17.80") or RemoteUrl has "xxooonline.eu.cc"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("137.175.93.126", "43.108.17.80") or DstHostname has "xxooonline.eu.cc" or Url has "xxooonline.eu.cc"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WP-SHELLSTORM primary webshell 'down.php' written under wp-content AIInstallation High
High-fidelity named-IOC rule for the campaign's main backdoor: a file literally named down.php (BestShell-derived, four-layer obfuscation) created anywhere under wp-content. Complements the behavioural PHP-drop hunt with a precise, alertable filename match. Rationale: The article and SOCRadar both name the main backdoor file 'down.php' (heavily obfuscated, BestShell-derived); a precise filename+path match is the cleanest alertable IOC even though no sample hash was published. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/exposed-hacker-server-reveals-wp.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate download-manager plugin coincidentally shipping a file named down.php (verify the file is not obfuscated)
  • A restore from backup re-creating a previously-planted down.php (still a true positive to remediate)
  • A developer using down.php as a maintenance-mode toggle script
  • Security tooling writing a decoy/canary named down.php
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the file - genuine down.php is four-layer obfuscated (nested base64_decode/gzinflate/eval); confirm and grab its SHA256 to seed a hash IOC. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, take the site into maintenance, and rotate site + DB + hosting-panel credentials. 3) Hunt: search all managed web hosts for the same SHA256 and for other webshells, review web access logs for POSTs to /wp-content/*/down.php to scope attacker command activity, and check the host for VShell/SNOWLIGHT and C2 callbacks.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "down.php"
| where FolderPath has "/wp-content/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "down.php"
| where TargetFilePath has "/wp-content/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-3844", "CVE-2026-48907", "CVE-2026-3300", "CVE-2026-1969", "CVE-2020-36847", "CVE-2026-6433", "CVE-2025-7443", "CVE-2026-0740", "CVE-2025-12057", "CVE-2025-7852", "CVE-2020-25213", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-3844", "CVE-2026-48907", "CVE-2026-3300", "CVE-2026-1969", "CVE-2020-36847", "CVE-2026-6433", "CVE-2025-7443", "CVE-2026-0740", "CVE-2025-12057", "CVE-2025-7852", "CVE-2020-25213", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
